transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 min
Attendees: Maya Chopra (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connell (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Support), Dr. Neha Raman (AstraSpan), Carlos Mendez (AstraSpan), Priya Shah (AstraSpan CTO)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC lab readout measuring latency and throughput vs AstraSpan's incumbent vendor. Focus on p50/p95 deltas, steady-state QPS, KV cache benefits, and routing/fallback behavior. Action items agreed to exchange raw traces and run a head-to-head load test.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, can folks hear me okay?
[00:06] Dr. Neha: Yep, heard you.
[00:09] Carlos: Good here.
[00:12] Maya: Cool. This is our weekly POC readout, we'll go through the lab results from last night's runs and compare against the baseline you shared. Liam will run through the numbers, then we'll talk tuning.
[00:25] Liam: Great — hi all. I'll start with a quick table: so on Redwood's side, test harness used model-7B-quant (approx) with KV prefix caching enabled, sequence length 512, workload mix matches the payloads you sent. P50 was 118 ms, P95 330 ms under target load (sustained 180 qps). Baseline provider numbers — using the configs you provided — were P50 ~210 ms, P95 ~490 ms at same sustained qps.
[00:52] Priya: Wait, those deltas are pretty big at p95 — did you all match batching and max tokens?
[01:00] Liam: Good call. We matched max_tokens to 256 and batching window settings to what was in your YAML. Small differences in the baseline: IncumbentAI appears to use a 20ms batching window and slightly smaller batch cap, which increases variability. Also our KV cache gave a substantial prefix hit rate — about 32% of requests benefited.
[01:20] Dr. Neha: When you say KV cache, do you mean the prefix cache in Redwood's runtime? Sometimes we see that get mis-attributed in logs.
[01:25] Liam: Yes, the prefix/KV cache in the runtime, the same cache that stores recent attention key/values. I'll note that some of the automated transcriptions earlier called it "K V cash" — sorry the export is messy. But functionally yes, cached prefixes reduced token generation time on repeated prompts.
[01:40] Maya: There were a few runs where we intentionally disabled caching to see cold behavior — Liam, can you speak to cold start and cold-cache numbers?
[01:48] Liam: Cold-cache p95 went up to ~720 ms on the heaviest model paths, but average cold-cache p50 stayed ~340 ms. That's still better than the baseline's cold p95 in their setup, which spiked to ~950-1,100 ms in our runs. The cold behavior is mostly influenced by KV population and model sharding.
[02:10] Carlos: Our biggest concern is steady-state 95th percentile under mixed traffic — do you have breakdowns by payload length? In our dataset we have a long tail of 1,200 token sequences.
[02:20] Liam: Yes — we bucketed by sequence: short (<128), mid (128–512), long (>512). Most of the delta versus baseline is in the long bucket. Redwood's kernel selection and attention optimizations give a 25–40% improvement in the long path. With quantization tuned, the long path p95 improved ~30% versus baseline.
[02:40] Priya: Hmm. One thing: the baseline provider uses their own optimized compiled kernels — are we sure the models are functionally identical (same ops and patching)?
[02:48] Maya: We documented the model variants in the spreadsheet — Liam, we used model-v1.7b-q4_0 and the baseline used their v1.7b-8bit variant. There are small representation differences, but we validated parity on the eval set. Error rates and answer drift were within the 1.2% window you set as acceptable.
[03:08] Dr. Neha: Good. On throughput numbers, can you show the steady-state QPS?
[03:12] Liam: Sure — under a sustained 180 qps with 70/20/10 short/mid/long mix, Redwood sustained 180 qps with p95 330 ms. Baseline hit ~150 qps before p95 rose beyond 500 ms. In a later run where we pushed up to 250 qps, Redwood started to throttle and fall back to a heavier instance class, p95 climbed to ~620 ms, but throughput held for a short window. Baseline at 250 qps blew past 800 ms p95 quickly.
[03:45] Carlos: Did those higher qps runs use burst capacity or reserved slots? We need to understand autoscaling behavior vs Dedicated slots.
[03:52] Liam: These were hosted runs using Redwood's shared pool with our burst policy — no Reserved Dedicated slots. For Dedicated you'd get much more predictable tail latencies; we can estimate the commit size needed for your SLA.
[04:05] Priya: Cost question — at steady-state what's the unit cost delta? Our CFO asked for tokens-per-dollar comparisons.
[04:12] Maya: We included unit economics in the spreadsheet: roughly on comparable model variants, Redwood's per-token inference cost is ~0.0023 USD per 1k tokens vs baseline's 0.0036 in their published pricing for that commit. That's before quantization and caching savings — effective cost can drop another 18–25% for your mix due to prefix cache.
[04:33] Dr. Neha: Nice. But we have to validate compliance — encryption at rest and KMS integration — the security review is part of our procurement.
[04:40] Maya: Absolutely — last week we shared the SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes. We'll re-send the security pack and the on-prem/private control plane options.
[04:50] Priya: Thanks. Back to benchmarks — you mentioned variability across regions? Our users are US-west heavy.
[04:56] Liam: All runs were in us-west-2 to match your profile. We did a quick eu-west run and saw ~15% higher latency p95 due to network hop differences. But for your use-case us-west is what matters.
[05:10] Carlos: A few things we noticed in your logs — there were spikes at 22:14 and 22:33 UTC — any idea?
[05:18] Jordan: That was when the batcher bumped up due to a burst from the synthetic generator — the harness injected an extra 40 concurrent short requests to exercise tail behavior. It skews the p95 a bit but that's intentional.
[05:28] Dr. Neha: Okay understood. I want to dig into the routing/fallback setup — our prod requirement is 99.95% under 500 ms for interactive features; fallback to a cheaper-but-slower model is okay but must be deterministic. How did Redwood's routing behave in the test?
[05:42] Liam: We exercised the routing policy that prefers low-latency instances and will fall back to a cost-tier model at a defined threshold. In our run we set fallback to start when instance queue latency exceeds 200 ms for more than 5s. Fallback occurred in the 250 qps push test and you can see the fallback timestamps in the trace. The fallback model added about 70–150 ms extra latency but preserved throughput and avoided errors.
[06:05] Priya: Are the fallbacks model-aware (semantic fallback) or just cheaper variants?
[06:10] Liam: Currently we route to compatible model variants (smaller width or lower quantization) that preserve API contract; semantic fallbacks (like returning cached responses) are configurable but off by default.
[06:20] Carlos: On KV cache— how often does cache warm-up occur, and does it persist across requests when we scale down to zero?
[06:28] Liam: Cache is per runtime instance and backed to an on-host store; if an instance is torn down cache is lost. We have strategies to pin instances (dedicated) to keep cache hot. For hosted runs with autoscale to zero you see cold-cache penalties.
[06:42] Dr. Neha: That matters — our usage pattern has periodic bursts after quiet windows, and we saw cold p95's earlier. I'd like to test a "pinned small pool" scenario.
[06:51] Maya: Good idea, we can spin up a small reserved pool to mimic pinning. Liam, add that to the head-to-head test plan?
[06:57] Liam: On it. I'll include a pinned pool run and autoscale-to-zero run.
[07:02] Priya: Also, quantization effects — you said q4_0 produced decent latency but how about quality?
[07:09] Liam: We ran the eval set and saw a 0.9% drop in exact-match on constrained tasks; on open-ended generation the human checks found no meaningful degradation. We can share the eval export.
[07:20] Dr. Neha: We require sample prompts to be run end-to-end, not just token-level diffs. Can you put together a small eval harness that runs our top 200 prompts and returns similarity metrics?
[07:30] Maya: Yes — we'll send the harness results with the next artifact upload.
[07:34] Carlos: About your throttling at 250 qps — when you switch to heavier instance class was that automatic? Any cold-add time for that scale-up?
[07:42] Liam: The switch is automatic but there is a short rebalancing window of 6–12s where queues can climb; autoscale to new instance types is fast but not instantaneous. For strict SLAs we recommend Reserved Dedicated slots sized for peak or aggressive warm-pools.
[07:56] Priya: Let's talk practical next steps — we need the raw traces, and a reproducible head-to-head test with exact same load generator seed.
[08:03] Maya: Agreed. Action items noted. We'll export the traces and a runbook describing the harness and seeds.
[08:08] Dr. Neha: Also, please include the precise city/region endpoints and any DNS variance — we saw a small jitter that might be due to DNS TTLs.
[08:15] Jordan: We'll include endpoint FQDNs and observed DNS resolution times in the trace meta.
[08:20] Maya: Quick question for AstraSpan — what's the internal timeline for making a decision and what stakeholders need the next artifact?
[08:26] Priya: We're on a two-week review window; security/compliance must sign off first, then platform and cost review. If the head-to-head looks good and security clears, procurement will start contract talks. So ideally we want the head-to-head and security answers this week.
[08:39] Maya: We'll prioritize that.
[08:41] Carlos: One nit — in the CSV there's a column "lat_ms_95" but I found a few rows with weird NaN entries around the big burst. Might be the harness.
[08:50] Liam: That's likely from aborted runs during the injection; I'll scrub and regenerate the CSV with cleaned aggregation.
[08:55] Dr. Neha: Can you surface percentile delta heatmaps? Visuals help the execs.
[08:59] Maya: Yes, we'll include a quick slide with delta heatmaps p50/p90/p95 across buckets.
[09:05] Priya: Also, pricing: can you produce a token-cost projection for our 6-month forecast? We'll need that for finance.
[09:11] Maya: Yes — finance-ready projection with cache-adjusted effective unit cost. We'll include assumptions and a sensitivity table.
[09:18] Carlos: For the head-to-head, we need identical model version and the same prompt canonicalization. Slight differences cause downstream drift.
[09:24] Liam: We'll run with your canonicalizer; please attach it to the shared drive.
[09:29] Dr. Neha: Sending it after the call.
[09:32] Priya: Great. A couple of technical clarifications — what metrics do you capture client-side vs server-side? Latency at app vs server processing time.
[09:40] Jordan: We collect server-side processing time, queue wait, model decode time, and total wall-clock including network. We'll annotate what you're seeing in your client logs.
[09:48] Carlos: Perfect.
[09:50] Maya: Any additional blockers?
[09:53] Dr. Neha: None besides the security docs and baseline config.
[09:56] Maya: OK let's recap.
[09:58] Maya: Recap: Redwood to share cleaned benchmark CSV, raw traces, delta heatmap slide, and pricing projection by 2026-05-07. AstraSpan to share baseline provider config and prompt canonicalizer by 2026-05-08. Redwood SE to run head-to-head 1-hour load test including pinned pool and autoscale-to-zero scenarios, deliver traces by 2026-05-11. Schedule deep-dive next week to examine cold starts and autoscale behavior.
[10:22] Priya: That aligns.
[10:24] Dr. Neha: Thanks all.
[10:26] Maya: I'll send meeting notes and the drive link after this. Appreciate the time.
[10:30] Carlos: Thanks.
[10:32] Liam: Thanks everyone.

(End of recording)
